sections.title: Begin tissue culture with a small explant
paragraphs: Micropropagation grows small pieces of plant tissue, called explants, in vitro: outside the parent plant in a controlled culture vessel. Start with a suitable parent showing the desired characteristics. Prepare small tissue pieces and place them aseptically on a suitable sterile nutrient medium; uncontrolled contamination can compete with or damage the culture.

The medium supplies water, mineral ions and usually a sugar source, with growth regulators chosen for the plant and stage. Suitable conditions allow living cells to divide by mitosis and develop new plant tissue. This is a description of the stages, not a home culturing recipe. An explant is plant tissue, not a fertilised seed, and in vitro does not mean planting in ordinary field soil.

example.question: Why are small explants placed on sterile medium using aseptic handling?
steps: The tissue needs suitable resources and conditions to grow.
Unwanted microbes can exploit the medium and interfere with plant growth.
Sterile medium and aseptic transfer reduce contamination; they do not by themselves prove the parent is free of every pathogen.
example.explanation: Resource supply and contamination control address different problems.

commonMistakes: Aseptic handling is not a guarantee that an explant already containing a pathogen is disease-free.

sections.title: Multiply shoots, establish roots and acclimatise plantlets
paragraphs: Develop growing tissue or shoots from the explant, divide suitable growing material and transfer it to fresh medium to multiply it. Adjust culture conditions and growth regulators for shoot formation and rooting as appropriate. Not every plant must pass through the same visible mass of undifferentiated tissue: the useful route depends on the material and species.

Once plantlets have suitable shoots and roots, transfer them out of culture and gradually acclimatise them to nursery conditions before wider planting. A protected vessel and an outdoor environment differ in humidity and other conditions, so abrupt transfer can cause losses. Mitosis maintains the parent’s inherited nuclear information through this asexual process, apart from changes such as mutations.

example.question: Outline the sequence from an explant to plants ready for nursery growth.
steps: Choose suitable parent tissue and establish it aseptically on suitable culture medium.
Multiply growing shoots or tissue and develop shoots and roots under appropriate conditions.
Separate suitable rooted plantlets and acclimatise them when transferred out of culture.
example.explanation: Multiplication, rooting and acclimatisation are distinct stages; an explant is not immediately a field-ready plant.

commonMistakes: Sexual fertilisation and meiosis are not the mechanism for multiplying this tissue culture.

sections.title: Copy a useful plant line without reshuffling its inheritance
paragraphs: Micropropagation can multiply a chosen plant line into many plants with the same inherited characteristics, rather than relying on seeds that may segregate or recombine parental alleles. This is useful when a nursery needs a large supply of a desirable variety, such as a selected flower form or crop line. It multiplies a useful line; it does not create the original breeding improvement.

The intended result is genetically identical plants, but mutations or changes arising during culture can produce off-types, so commercial material must be checked. Shared inheritance also does not guarantee identical size or yield in different environments. Producing one uniform line does not add genetic diversity and can leave many plants vulnerable to the same disease; skilled culture, contamination control and acclimatisation add costs and possible losses.

example.question: Why might a nursery use tissue culture after breeding a plant with a useful flower form?
steps: The selected line already carries the useful inherited combination.
Asexual tissue multiplication can retain that combination without the reshuffling involved in seed production.
Repeated multiplication can supply many plants, but quality, contamination, cost and survival still need checking.
example.explanation: The benefit is copying the chosen line at scale, with conditions and limitations.

commonMistakes: Genetically similar plants can still show environmental differences, and culture does not guarantee zero mutations.

sections.title: Count saleable plants, not just theoretical multiplication
paragraphs: Commercial output depends on both multiplication and the fraction of plantlets that survive later stages and meet quality criteria. Starting explants, multiplied shoots, rooted plantlets and saleable plants are different counts. Record the stage to which a survival percentage applies before calculating an output.

Compare methods using consistent starting material, time and quality criteria. A higher shoot count can be offset by contamination, poor rooting or low survival after transfer. These counts describe propagation success; they do not demonstrate that a new inherited trait has been created or that every plant is genetically identical.

example.question: An invented nursery starts with 20 viable explants. Two rounds each give three usable shoots per starting piece, with no losses during those rounds. All 180 shoots root; 80% then survive acclimatisation and pass quality checks. Find the saleable output.
steps: After the first round: 20 × 3 = 60.
After the second round: 60 × 3 = 180.
Saleable plants: 180 × 0.80 = 144.
This assumes the stated multiplication and rooting success; change the assumptions if losses occur earlier.
example.explanation: Invented values illustrate stages and assumptions. They are not a measured propagation rate or a promise of commercial performance.

commonMistakes: Do not apply a survival percentage to the original explant count when it refers to the later plantlet stage.

sections.title: Transfer a mature diploid nucleus into an enucleated egg
paragraphs: In the mammalian cloning model, obtain a diploid nucleus from a mature body cell of the animal to be copied. Remove the nucleus from a recipient unfertilised egg cell, leaving its cytoplasm. Place the mature-cell nucleus into the enucleated egg, or combine the mature cell with that egg so that its nucleus is transferred.

Activate the reconstructed cell to begin development. If it develops successfully, early divisions form an embryo that can be transferred into a suitable surrogate mother’s uterus. Continued pregnancy and birth are later stages, not guaranteed outcomes. No sperm nucleus is combined with the donor nucleus in this process. Dolly illustrates development from an adult mammary-cell nuclear donor; she was the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell, rather than the first mammal ever cloned.

example.question: Why must the recipient egg nucleus be removed before transfer of the mature body-cell nucleus?
steps: The egg’s own nucleus contains its nuclear genetic information.
Removing it allows the diploid donor nucleus to provide the intended nuclear genome.
Leaving both nuclei would not be the specified nuclear-transfer cloning process.
example.explanation: Enucleated means nucleus removed, not cytoplasm removed or an empty cell with no useful components.

commonMistakes: The diploid nucleus comes from a mature body cell, not from a sperm cell.

diagram.alt: Body-cell donor provides a diploid nucleus; egg donor provides cytoplasm after nucleus removal. Nuclear transfer and activation precede embryo development, then transfer to a surrogate; the surrogate is not the nuclear donor.
diagram.caption: Original nuclear-transfer model for Paper 2B. Successful development is conditional; nuclear inheritance, egg contribution and pregnancy are distinct.

sections.title: Separate the nuclear donor, egg donor and surrogate
paragraphs: The mature-cell donor supplies the nuclear genetic information copied in this model. The egg donor supplies a recipient cell with cytoplasm and organelles after its nucleus is removed. The surrogate provides the environment for embryo development during pregnancy; it does not supply another nucleus through fertilisation.

At syllabus level the offspring is called a genetic clone of the nuclear donor. More precisely, nuclear DNA is copied from that donor, while mitochondria and their DNA are mainly supplied by the recipient egg. Gene activity, development and the environment can also differ. A clone is a new young organism, not the donor’s existing body, memories or exact appearance at its present age.

example.question: In an invented case, animal A supplies the body-cell nucleus, B supplies the enucleated egg and C carries the pregnancy. Whose nuclear information is copied?
steps: A is the source of the transferred nuclear information.
B supplies the egg cytoplasm and predominantly its mitochondrial contribution.
C supports pregnancy; C is not the nuclear donor in the stated process.
example.explanation: Track what each participant contributes rather than assigning all inheritance to whichever animal gives birth.

commonMistakes: A shared nuclear genome does not make every molecule, developmental event or environment identical.

sections.title: Distinguish attempted transfers from successful births
paragraphs: A nuclear-transfer attempt can fail before an embryo develops, during pregnancy or at another stage. A useful description of success states the starting group and the outcome counted. “Embryos developing” and “healthy live births” are different measures, and the percentage changes if the denominator is changed.

Cloning is technically demanding and development is not guaranteed. A comparison needs appropriate records, outcome definitions and welfare considerations. One success does not show every attempt works; one failed attempt does not show the method can never work. Do not infer that a clone automatically has the donor’s age or remaining lifespan.

example.question: Invented records: 40 reconstructed eggs, 10 developing embryos, two live births. Calculate embryo development per reconstructed egg, births per embryo and births per reconstructed egg.
steps: Developing embryos: 10 ÷ 40 × 100 = 25%.
Live births per developing embryo: 2 ÷ 10 × 100 = 20%.
Live births per reconstructed egg: 2 ÷ 40 × 100 = 5%.
example.explanation: These invented rates are not Dolly’s experimental results or a current real-world success estimate. State the denominator.

commonMistakes: Calling the final success rate 20% without its denominator hides the earlier losses.

sections.title: A transgenic animal can express a human protein
paragraphs: A transgenic animal can carry introduced coding DNA for a human protein, arranged with suitable control sequences so that chosen tissues express it. For example, expression in a mammary gland can release a target protein into milk. The animal’s cells make the protein from the introduced information; transferring human DNA does not turn the animal into a human.

If a productive animal is cloned using a suitable transgenic body-cell nucleus, the transferred nuclear genome can copy the inserted sequence into further animals. Product formation still requires the right tissues and expression conditions. Collect the relevant material, recover and purify the target protein, then check identity and quality. Milk containing a target protein is not itself a finished medicine, and cloning alone does not insert the human coding sequence.

example.question: In a hypothetical teaching model, a transgenic animal expresses a human protein labelled P in milk. Explain how cloning and purification play different roles.
steps: Genetic modification establishes the introduced coding information and suitable expression controls.
Nuclear-transfer cloning can copy that established genetic arrangement into further animals.
Expressing animals produce P; recovery, purification and quality checks separate the intended product from the collected material.
example.explanation: This is a hypothetical teaching model. It does not claim that a particular approved product uses cloning or that every clone has the same output.

commonMistakes: An animal being a clone is not evidence that it is transgenic; its donor must carry the introduced sequence.

sections.title: Modification establishes an arrangement; cloning copies it
paragraphs: Compare the mechanisms rather than treating useful outcomes as equivalent. Selective breeding chooses parents and descendants over generations. Genetic modification changes genetic information directly. Cross-species transfer makes a transgenic example under this specification. Cloning copies a chosen genetic arrangement through an asexual route.

An organism can be both cloned and transgenic if the copied donor already contains introduced DNA from a different species. An ordinary clone need not be transgenic, and sexual descendants of a transgenic organism need not be clones. For protein manufacture, copying the arrangement and producing a purified working product remain separate tasks.

example.question: A mature body cell from an animal containing human coding DNA supplies a nucleus for cloning. Which operations created the cross-species arrangement and which copied it?
steps: Earlier genetic modification introduced the human coding DNA and established the transgenic arrangement.
The later cloning operation copies the donor nuclear arrangement.
Production and purification of the intended protein are subsequent operations, not the same as either DNA transfer or cloning.
example.explanation: This explanation connects definitions without treating a shared useful trait as proof of a shared method.

commonMistakes: Cloning does not introduce a transgene merely because the resulting organism is useful.
